rules.title: A lens, not an identity.
bodyLines: The 16 codes are one of several vocabularies people use to talk
about themselves. Decades of peer-reviewed work find the MBTI's dichotomies psychometrically
weak: scores cluster near the midpoints, test–retest type changes within weeks are common, and
predictive validity for behavior is modest at best — the 2021 JSTOR systematic review and
meta-analysis found "reasonable construct validity" only in the loose sense, with weak
test–retest and criterion performance ([JSTOR systematic review](https://www.jstor.org/stable/26554264);
[PMC leadership-behavior review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10017728/)).
The official publisher's own validity page is a vendor claim, not independent evidence
([myersbriggs.org](https://www.myersbriggs.org/research-and-library/validity-reliability/)).

rules.title: Name the tactic, not the person.
bodyLines: "Guilt followed by urgency" is an observable behavior you
can act on. "They are a narcissist" is a verdict that forecloses evidence and that you are not
qualified to make — no checklist here, and no personality test anywhere, can diagnose another
person, and the research measures behind the Dark Triad name are validated only as
*self-report trait scales in studies*, never as remote assessments
([Cognitive Empathy and the Dark Triad review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10670677/)).
This app provides no tool for labeling someone else and will not build one.

rules.title: Patterns, not incidents.
bodyLines: Everyone is occasionally selfish, charming, or unfair. What this
guide catalogs as a *pattern* is trajectory: repetition, escalation, and — most diagnostic of
all — what happens when you hold a boundary. A single incident is information; a pattern is a
different thing. Your observation log (`DESIGN-personal-defense-profile.md` §3), not this page,
decides whether the pattern describes your situation.
